title: Rabbi Avin (II)

paragraphs: Hyman writes: In the Jerusalem Talmud he is always called R' Bun, and in the Babylonian Talmud R' Avin. His father was also a Torah scholar who taught baraitot, and he is called "the father of R' Avin," as in Gittin ch. 5: "Avuha de-R' Avin taught before R' Zeira." The son, R' Bun [the subject of this entry], apparently also received teachings from Rabbi Zeira, as in Shekalim, end of ch. 4: "R' Avun and R' Bun asked before Rabbi Zeira [supplied ר״ז]." He likewise spoke in the name of R' Berekhya, as in Vayikra Rabbah ch. 34-16, in the name of R' Berekhya Sava (Vayikra Rabbah ch. 1-4), in the name of R' Yehuda bar R' Simon (Vayikra Rabbah ch. 28-6), and in the name of R' Pinchas (Shekalim, beginning of ch. 7). He was the head of the academy in Tiberias, as in Kohelet Rabbah ch. 11-2. It is told of him in Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot ch. 5, halakha 1, that he once went in before the royal authority, and when he left he turned his face away as he went out (this is not proper conduct before the king: he should have walked backwards); they sought to kill him, but they saw two sparks of fire coming out with him and let him go.

Hyman relates that he died during the intermediate days of a festival, per Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan ch. 3, halakha 7 (in the city of Tiberias, per Kohelet Rabbah ch. 10-2; and by then R' Mana, son of R' Yona, was already head in the city of Sepphoris). R' Mana did not do him the kindness (of eulogizing him), and the Sepphoris people said, 'He must have hated him until death' (that R' Mana hated him). After the festival R' Mana paid him honor, entered and said before them: As taught, 'When a sage dies, all are his relatives' — those who were with him; we were not with him (so they did not eulogize him during the festival). He left behind a son great in Torah, known as R' Yose bar R' Bun, a student of R' Mana, as explained in his entry.

notes.text: Hyman's printed abbreviation 'ר"ז' (in 'R' Avun and R' Bun asked before R. Z.') is rendered 'R. Z.' literally; the preceding sentence names R' Zeira, but the abbreviation is left as printed. 'ב'ל"ס'-type and other Hebrew abbreviations (e.g., ד"א, ת"ח, ג"כ) rendered by plain sense; 'ד"א' is expanded as 'derekh eretz' as a likely reading, uncertain.

The Aramaic fragment 'ובעו למקטליה וראו ב' זקוקין דנוא דנפיק ושבקוהו' and Hyman's parenthetical about not walking backwards before the king are translated as plain sense; the identity of 'the royal authority' (קומי מלכותא) is left as printed.

The Aramaic phrase 'עבד ליא איקריה' is rendered as 'made an honor-gathering for him'; this is an uncertain rendering of a difficult idiom. The sentence containing 'באינון דהוון גביה' is rendered per Hyman's parenthetical explanation.

The whole saved Guggenheimer Berakhot 5:1 Hebrew paragraph names Rabbi Avun and describes turning his neck and two sparks of fire from his neck. Hyman’s face wording and supplied דנוא remain unchanged and held; no emperor, migration or tefillin identification from the accompanying commentary is imported. The fresh whole Guggenheimer Shekalim 4:4 paragraphs explicitly name Rabbi Avin and Rabbi Zeura, locally supporting the heading and the Shekalim ר״ז expansion as Rabbi Zeira with the supplied siglum visible. The digital question names Rabbi Bun and Rabbi Bun, whereas Hyman supplies Avun and Bun; those forms are kept distinct. The two whole 4:5 paragraphs do not contain that exchange; this bounded comparison does not repair Hyman’s end-of-chapter locator. Avin’s father teaches a baraita in Gittin 53a, in chapter 5. The words about teaching before Rabbi Zeira occur in the consulted Gittin 85a, where Zeira questions the ruling and it is restated. Hyman I, pp. 92–93, combines the chapter 5 pointer with the words about Zeira. The printed notice reads דנור, ‘of fire’, where the supplied Hebrew has דנוא. In the consulted Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 5:1 the figure is named Rabbi Avun, turns his neck, and the two sparks come from his neck. Hyman writes that he turns his face away. The two Bun names and the form Zeura in the Shekalim 4:4 exchange are local readings. Hyman’s apparently and always remain part of his own account.

The consulted Vayikra Rabbah 34:16 has Avin in Berekhya’s name, 1:4 has Avin in Berekhya Sava’s name, and 28:6 names Avun and two other transmitters in Yehuda son of Rabbi Simon’s name. Shekalim 7:1 names Avun in Rabbi Pinchas’s name. In the consulted Kohelet Rabbah 11:3, Rabbi Mona in Sepphoris and Rabbi Bun in Tiberias are examples in a passage about where a sage dies. Hyman’s chapter references and inference about headship are preserved. Jerusalem Talmud Moed Katan 3:7 names Avun and Mana, records the accusation by the people of Sepphoris, and gives Mana’s explanation after the festival about those who had been with the sage. Hyman’s account of their offices, the deceased’s family and his son’s studies remains attributed.
